source.title: Scaling Data-Constrained Language Models
source.authors: B. Barak; Teven Le Scao; Niklas Muennighoff; Aleksandra Piktus; Sampo Pyysalo; Colin A. Raffel; Alexander M. Rush; Nouamane Tazi; Thomas Wolf

page_placements.theme: Limited data can make smaller language models preferable

record.tranche_reason: The authors train language models and measure held-out loss over training epochs, directly testing an epoch-wise double-descent pattern on new model and data settings. They also vary model size, though some size comparisons change size and epochs together.
record.gate_note: The paper's own epoch-wise loss curves and parameter-scaling results are included. Results cited from prior work are not rows. The authors' fitted scaling-law coefficients are not outcomes; the reported model-size and epoch results are recorded below.
record.test_reason: Appendix D reports final test loss against epoch count for 14M, 44M and 83M GPT-2 models on 100M unique C4 tokens. The authors call the result epoch-wise double descent: loss rises around 200 epochs, then falls again. This is a new setting (language-model pretraining, cross-entropy loss) bearing on V2. It is a side observation, not the paper's focus. Each point is a separate run trained to completion with a cosine schedule, not a single training trajectory. The model-size results (r1, r2) do not isolate size or locate an interpolation threshold, so they do not test V1.
record.authors_conclusion: Partly right, but it misplaces the emphasis. The main conclusions are about data repetition and scaling laws. Up to about 4 epochs of repeated data is nearly as good as unique data, and returns decay sharply beyond about 16 epochs. A fitted data-constrained scaling law favours scaling epochs faster than parameters, and adding code gives about 2x more effective data. Epoch-wise double descent is an appendix observation, which the authors treat as noise and remove from their fits. They attribute excess parameters or epochs hurting to suboptimal regularization.
record.recipe_differences: Uses GPT-2-architecture language models and held-out language-model loss, with repeated-data epoch sweeps and scaling experiments; it does not reproduce the full original set of axes and settings.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported size and epoch behavior depends on the data budget and whether parameter count and epochs are varied jointly; the paper also notes hyperparameter sensitivity as a limitation.

fits_no_version.finding: At fixed 100M unique tokens, increasing parameters and epochs together first lowers test loss by over 50%. The best loss comes at about 20-60x the compute-optimal parameters and epochs, after which loss increases again.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In data-constrained LM pretraining, jointly scaling parameters and epochs gives a U-shaped test loss with no reported second descent.

fits_no_version.finding: Single-epoch models on 100M tokens above 2B parameters have significantly higher test loss than 200M-1B models, under both default and µP hyperparameters.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Excess parameters raise test loss in severely data-limited single-epoch pretraining; hyperparameter transfer (µP) does not prevent it.

record.problems: The epoch-wise double-descent evidence is described qualitatively and shown in plots without reported numeric loss values or uncertainty bars, and it covers three model sizes on one data budget. The parameter-size evidence does not isolate size in the main sweep; the single-epoch comparison reports a harmful-size range but not a complete double-descent curve.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant reported outcomes were left out.

untested.parts: All of it: there is no size-only sweep across an interpolation threshold and no second descent at larger sizes.
Other model sizes, other data budgets, label noise, and within-run training trajectories. Only three small models on 100M C4 tokens are reported.
All of it: GPT-2 transformers only.
All of it. The authors only hypothesize that regularization would prevent excess parameters from hurting; µP did not remove the effect, and dropout was not tuned.
All of it. The paper's 'effective parameters' term is a fitted scaling-law construct that is not used to re-plot the curve.

missing.what: 146M-parameter models on 100M C4 tokens, regular vs deduplicated, final test loss across 27-1740 epochs. Optimum is at 59 epochs. The text does not say whether a second descent appears; the figure would bear on V2 at another model size.
Statement that some runs show loss increasing midway through training (e.g. 44-epoch IsoFLOP models), with no later recovery reported. These are within-run epoch curves at billion-parameter scale.

record.verdict_notes: Tranche changed from T1 to T3: the setting is LM pretraining with cross-entropy loss, not the original image classifiers with label noise. V1 labels were dropped because neither size row isolates model size or locates an interpolation threshold. Neither original source is this paper.

versions.untested_parts: The joint parameter-and-epoch sweep does not isolate model size, and the single-epoch comparison does not establish a peak near an interpolation threshold followed by a second descent at still larger sizes.
The explicitly reported epoch-wise double descent covers three model sizes trained on 100 million unique tokens; it does not establish the pattern across other datasets or training setups.
The study varies unique-data budgets and repetition, but does not test increasing sample size near an interpolation threshold.
The experiments use GPT-2-architecture language models, not a broad range of model classes.
The proposed fit uses separate decay terms for data repetitions and excess parameters; the study does not test whether one effective-complexity measure predicts peak locations across axes.
The study does not test whether label noise or variance drives the peak, whether multiple peaks occur, or whether optimally tuned regularization removes it.
The study does not test whether counting complexity by an effective parameter count converts the second descent into an ordinary U-shaped curve.

rows.subject: GPT-2 architecture language models (93 models; aggregate sweep)
rows.operation_detail: Vary model parameters and epochs at fixed unique-data budget
rows.baseline: one-epoch compute-optimal model; figure shows loss 8.10
rows.value: More than a 50% reduction in loss was attained by training for several epochs and increasing model size beyond the one-epoch compute-optimal size; best loss was around 20-60× more parameters and epochs.
rows.note: The text reports the trend but varies size and epochs jointly; it does not establish a size-only double-descent curve.
rows.check: The sweep varies parameters and epochs jointly, so it cannot show a model-wise curve or an interpolation-threshold peak. The 8.10 baseline is the 7M one-epoch point, and the value is a gain relative to that point, not a test of V1. The authors add that loss eventually rises again as both grow. This is a related finding, recorded under fits_no_version.

rows.subject: GPT-2 architecture language models (parameter sweep)
rows.size_stated: 200 million to more than 2 billion parameters, as described in text
rows.operation_detail: Compare model sizes at one epoch and fixed data budget
rows.baseline: models with 200 million to 1 billion parameters
rows.value: Models with more than 2 billion parameters have significantly higher validation loss than models with 200 million to 1 billion parameters.
rows.note: The paper reports that excess parameters hurt in this tested range; it does not identify an interpolation threshold or a later second descent.
rows.check: These are single-epoch runs (about 250M to over 2B parameters) on 100M tokens, under default and µP hyperparameters. Models of this size likely do not interpolate the training set after one epoch, and no interpolation threshold is identified. A rise without a later fall in this range cannot speak to V1's peak or second descent. The authors attribute the rise to missing regularization. Labeling it reversed for V1 is unsupported; it is moved to fits_no_version.
